topic: Miscellaneous short notes: a generalisation of ratio-type convergence criteria for series, a recursion for a number in Hilbert's note on discriminant surfaces, a note on Cayley's problem, the parameter bound for intransitive projective groups, and normal forms of vector fields under analytic coordinate changes.

triage.modern_statement: Too fragmentary to identify. The note reads only "Problem der Cayley's[?]" ("Cayley's problem"). The transcription is marked uncertain, and there is no formula, object or context to go with it. Several different questions are called "Cayley's problem" in the literature. Examples are Cayley's 1879 question about the basins of attraction of Newton's method for complex polynomials (later studied through Julia sets), a combinatorial counting problem treated under that name in expository books, and possibly questions from Cayley's invariant theory, such as counting invariants or covariants (Cayley–Sylvester). That last one might seem to fit the nearby notes on discriminant surfaces and projective groups, but nothing on the page shows which one Hilbert meant.
triage.answered_by: Cannot be determined, because the problem cannot be identified. If it were Cayley's Newton's-method problem: complex dynamics (Fatou–Julia theory, and later Peitgen, Saupe and von Haeseler, 1984) showed that the basin boundaries for cubics and higher-degree polynomials are fractal Julia sets. Nothing ties Hilbert's note to that problem.

evidence.claim: A paper titled 'Cayley's problem and Julia sets' (Peitgen, Saupe, von Haeseler) treats Cayley's Newton's-method basin problem, which shows one established meaning of the phrase
A separate paper also titled 'Cayley's problem' (Applications of Mathematics, 1990) is about a difference equation and Newton's method, which shows the phrase is used for more than one question
'Cayley's Problem' is also a chapter title in the expository book The Art of Mathematics – Take Two, a different, combinatorial use of the name

triage.why: The entry is just a title with a doubtful reading and no mathematical content. Several unrelated problems are called 'Cayley's problem', and the neighbouring notes on the page don't settle which one Hilbert meant. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th. Linking it to any particular later solution would be speculation.
